Which portfolio entry would best show both her creative development and the computational artifact she helped create?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.optionA: A polished screenshot of the finished planner with a title and description, but no record of earlier concepts or design choices.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.optionB: A dated page showing several interface concepts, why one was selected, and a short demonstration of the feature Lina implemented.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.optionC: A complete copy of the team’s source code, without identifying Lina’s contribution or the ideas considered before coding.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.optionD: A list of every idea discussed by the team, without connecting any idea to the finished planner or showing the implemented feature.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.explanation:
Option B connects Lina’s ideation to a design decision and provides evidence of the feature she implemented, making the portfolio informative about both the development process and the resulting artifact.

Option A shows the final artifact but omits the creative development that led to it.

Option C includes the team’s code but does not show Lina’s contribution or the development of the design.

Option D records ideas but does not show how they informed the artifact or what Lina created.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.question: A student team is creating an interactive digital exhibit. They plan work in weekly development cycles, but for three cycles in a row, the team has completed only about half of the work it planned. The team wants to improve its development process without abandoning the exhibit’s goal. Which action is most likely to help?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.optionA: Review records from the cycles to identify why work took longer than expected, then use that information to plan a realistic amount of work for the next cycle.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.optionB: Keep the same plan, move unfinished work into the next cycle, and add extra tasks to make up for the repeated delays.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.optionC: Stop reviewing the artifact during development and evaluate it only after every planned feature has been completed.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.optionD: Replace the exhibit with a different idea so the team can avoid delays associated with the current project.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.explanation:
A is correct because the team can use evidence from completed cycles to adjust its planning process. This makes future cycles more realistic while keeping the project goal intact.

B is incorrect because carrying unfinished work forward while adding more tasks repeats the planning problem rather than addressing it.

C is incorrect because postponing evaluation removes opportunities to learn during development and makes the process less responsive.

D is incorrect because changing the project idea does not address the recurring difficulty in planning work.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.question: A student team plans to create a computational artifact that organizes volunteer shifts. Before building the complete artifact, the team is unsure whether its chosen data format will support the updates needed when volunteers trade shifts. Which action best uses a development cycle to address this uncertainty?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.optionA: Build a small prototype that tests shift trades with the chosen data format, then use the result to guide the next design step.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.optionB: Build every planned feature first, then decide whether the data format supports shift trades after the artifact is complete.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.optionC: Add more features to the design plan so the data format will be less important to the finished artifact.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.optionD: Document the original design in a portfolio and treat that documentation as evidence that the data format will work.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.explanation:
A small prototype tests a specific design assumption early. The team can use what it learns to revise its approach before investing in the complete artifact, which is an effective development cycle.

B postpones testing until changes may be more costly. C does not resolve the uncertainty about the data format. D documents the design but does not test whether it works.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.question: A student creates a computational artifact that estimates how much water a community garden needs each week. The student’s portfolio is intended to help next year’s volunteers understand and use the artifact. Which portfolio item would be most useful for that audience?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.optionA: A guide that explains the artifact’s purpose, required inputs, meaning of its outputs, and important assumptions
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.optionB: A chronological list of every coding session, including the time each session began and ended
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.optionC: A copy of the final program with all variable names replaced by shorter abbreviations
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.optionD: A collection of unrelated garden photographs that inspired the student to begin the project
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.explanation:
A portfolio can help an audience understand a computational artifact, not just preserve the artifact itself. A guide describing its purpose, inputs, outputs, and assumptions lets volunteers interpret its results and recognize how to use it appropriately.

A is correct because it communicates how the artifact is intended to be used and what its results mean.

B is incorrect because a session log records work times but does not explain how to use or interpret the artifact.

C is incorrect because shortening variable names makes the program harder to understand and provides no usage guidance.

D is incorrect because inspirational images do not explain the artifact’s function or how volunteers should use it.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.question: A student is designing a mobile app that helps users prepare for severe weather. Before writing the program, the student wants a planning artifact that shows the sequence of screens, the buttons on each screen, and how a user moves through the app from start to finish. Which planning artifact is most appropriate for this purpose?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.optionA: A storyboard, because it shows the order of screens and user interactions in the app
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.optionB: A data table, because it stores the weather alerts that the app will display
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.optionC: A test case list, because it records whether each feature works after the app is built
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.optionD: A citation list, because it documents the sources used to research severe weather
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-1.explanation:
A storyboard is the best choice because it is a planning tool used in creative development to visualize the sequence of screens and the user's path through the computational artifact before implementation. It helps the designer think through navigation and missing steps early.

B is incorrect because a data table organizes information, but it does not show the flow of screens or interactions.

C is incorrect because test cases are used later to check whether the finished artifact works as intended, not to plan the interface structure.

D is incorrect because citations document sources, which may be useful in a portfolio or report, but they do not help plan the app's user experience.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.question: A team randomly selects nine page-load times, in seconds, for each of two website configurations. Configuration A produces $2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 20$ seconds, while configuration B produces $4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4$ seconds. The team wants to choose the configuration with the faster *typical* page load and will investigate unusually slow loads separately. Which conclusion is best supported by these data?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.optionA: Choose configuration A: its median is $3$ seconds, compared with $4$ seconds for B; investigate the unusually slow A load separately.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.optionB: Choose configuration B: its mean is $4$ seconds, compared with $5$ seconds for A, so B has the faster typical load.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.optionC: Choose configuration A after removing the $20$-second observation, since unusually large observations should not affect comparisons.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.optionD: Treat the configurations as equivalent because configuration A’s one unusually slow load offsets its faster observations.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.explanation:
The median is a useful measure of a typical value when a dataset contains an extreme observation. Configuration A’s median is $3$ seconds, while configuration B’s is $4$ seconds, so the sample supports choosing A for a faster typical load. The $20$-second result should be retained and investigated rather than silently discarded. Because the samples are limited, the team should avoid claiming that every load on A will be faster.
A is correct: it compares the medians and treats the unusual observation as data worth investigating.
B is incorrect: the mean for A is increased by its one unusually slow load, so it does not represent the typical load as well in this scenario.
C is incorrect: there is no evidence that the $20$-second measurement is an error, and removing it without justification would distort the data.
D is incorrect: the median comparison shows that the typical observed load differs, even though A also has an unusually slow observation.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.question: A school data team creates a bar chart showing the number of students who checked out laptops each month: January, $198$; February, $201$; March, $204$; and April, $207$. The chart’s vertical axis begins at $195$, and the team says laptop checkouts rose sharply. Which change would make the chart support a more accurate conclusion?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.optionA: Start the vertical axis at zero and note that checkouts increased by $9$ from January to April.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.optionB: Keep the current axis but add the exact count above each bar so the visual comparison is reliable.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.optionC: Convert each month’s count to its share of the four-month total and use a pie chart to show the trend.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.optionD: Rescale the monthly counts so January is $0$ and April is $100$, then compare the resulting bars.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.explanation:
A bar chart’s bar lengths are compared from the axis baseline. Starting the axis at $195$ makes the bars look much more different than the counts are; starting at zero shows the modest increase of $9$ checkouts, about $4.5\%$ of January’s count.

A: Correct. A zero baseline represents the counts proportionally and supports a suitably cautious conclusion.
B: Exact labels provide useful information, but they do not remove the visual exaggeration caused by the truncated axis.
C: A pie chart shows each month’s share of the total, not the month-to-month trend, and is not the best representation for this comparison.
D: Rescaling the minimum and maximum to $0$ and $100$ exaggerates the differences rather than preserving the original counts’ relative sizes.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.question: A greenhouse system is scheduled to record humidity once per day. One week, its readings are $42$, $44$, missing because the sensor was disconnected, $46$, and $43$. A dashboard is designed to report the mean of the available readings and show whether any readings are missing. Which data-handling approach best supports an accurate report?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.optionA: Replace the missing reading with $0$ and calculate the mean using all five values.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.optionB: Keep the third reading marked as missing, calculate a mean of $43.75$ from the four recorded values, and flag the incomplete data.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.optionC: Copy the second day's reading into the third day, then calculate a mean using all five values.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.optionD: Discard all five readings because one day's value is unavailable, and report no mean for the week.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.explanation:
The missing entry means no humidity measurement was collected; it does not indicate a humidity of $0$. The mean of the four observed readings is $(42+44+46+43)/4=43.75$. Keeping the missing value distinct and noting the incomplete record makes the transformation transparent and prevents the dashboard from implying complete data.

A is incorrect because treating missing data as an actual $0$ would lower the mean and misrepresent what was measured.

C is incorrect because copying a previous reading invents a measurement and can distort the result.

D is incorrect because the four valid readings can still be summarized; the report should disclose the missing entry rather than discard all collected data.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.question: A library system compares daily checkout totals across branches when planning staff schedules. Each successful checkout receives a unique transaction ID, but a network retry can cause the same transaction to appear more than once in the log. The Tuesday log for one branch contains four rows: TX41 at 9:10 for member 008 and book K; TX42 at 9:10 for member 008 and book K; TX41 at 9:10 for member 008 and book K; and TX43 at 9:18 for member 015 and book M. Which data transformation produces the most reliable checkout total for that day?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.optionA: Keep one row per distinct transaction ID, then count the IDs; the total is 3.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.optionB: Keep one row per distinct member, time, and book combination; the total is 2.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.optionC: Count every row in the log because each row represents a recorded checkout; the total is 4.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.optionD: Remove every transaction ID that occurs more than once, then count the remaining rows; the total is 2.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.explanation:
A is correct: the transaction ID identifies a successful checkout, so keeping one row per distinct ID removes the retry duplicate while preserving TX42, a separate checkout with the same member, time, and book details. There are 3 distinct IDs.
B is incorrect because different transactions can share member, time, and book fields, so collapsing those rows can undercount.
C is incorrect because a retried transmission creates an extra log row for TX41, inflating the total.
D is incorrect because repeated appearance of an ID signals a duplicate row, not an invalid transaction; removing all rows with repeated IDs would discard the valid checkout TX41.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.question: An emergency-response agency combines dispatch logs from several regions. Each record stores a local date and time together with its UTC offset. Analysts want to calculate the elapsed time from dispatch to arrival for each incident and compare typical response times across regions. Which data transformation best supports a valid comparison?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.optionA: Convert each timestamp to UTC before calculating elapsed time, while retaining the original time and offset for local reporting.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.optionB: Remove the UTC offsets and subtract the displayed clock times, since each record already uses a consistent time format.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.optionC: Convert every timestamp using the offset from one selected region, so that all records follow the same regional clock.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.optionD: Group incidents by their recorded local dates and compare the displayed arrival times with the displayed dispatch times.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-2.explanation:
Timestamps with different UTC offsets can display different clock times for the same instant. Converting both dispatch and arrival timestamps to a common reference such as UTC before calculating each duration makes the calculations comparable; retaining the original values preserves useful context for local reporting.

A is correct because it standardizes the instants before calculating elapsed time without discarding the original information.

B is incorrect because equal-looking time formats do not make the timestamps comparable when their offsets differ.

C is incorrect because applying one region’s offset to every record changes the represented instants for records from other regions.

D is incorrect because local dates and clock times alone do not reliably establish elapsed duration across different offsets.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.question:
A game awards $3$ points for a round with a score of at least $8$ and $1$ point otherwise. The following procedures are intended to calculate the total points for a list of round scores.

```text
PROCEDURE pointsForRound(score)
  IF score >= 8
    RETURN 3
  ELSE
    RETURN 1
  END IF
END PROCEDURE

PROCEDURE totalPoints(scores)
  total <- 0
  FOR EACH score IN scores
    pointsForRound(score)
  RETURN total
END PROCEDURE
```

For the list `[6, 9, 8, 2]`, which replacement for the line `pointsForRound(score)` correctly makes `totalPoints` return the total points earned?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.explanation:
A is correct because `pointsForRound(score)` returns the points earned in one round, and adding that returned value to `total` accumulates the award for each round. The list earns $1 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 8$ points.

B replaces the running total on each iteration, so it keeps only the award from the last round.

C adds each raw score rather than the points returned by the helper procedure.

D displays each round's award but does not update `total`, so the procedure still returns $0$.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.optionA: It becomes about $4$ times as large.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.optionB: It becomes about $2$ times as large.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.optionC: It becomes about $100$ times as large.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.explanation:
With no duplicates, the procedure compares each pair exactly once. For a list of length $n$, the number of comparisons is $1 + 2 + \cdots + (n-1) = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$. Doubling $n$ therefore makes the comparison count approximately $4$ times as large.

A: Correct. The number of comparisons grows approximately with the square of the list length.

B: Incorrect. This would describe work that grows approximately in direct proportion to the list length.

C: Incorrect. Doubling the input does not multiply the number of comparisons by $100$; the nested loops produce approximately quadratic growth.

D: Incorrect. The loops perform many more comparisons when the list is longer.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.question:
A student is building a school-event flyer generator in AP CSP pseudocode. The student writes one procedure that creates a flyer using a title, date, and room number.

```
PROCEDURE MakeFlyer(title, date, room)
{
    DISPLAY(title)
    DISPLAY(date)
    DISPLAY(room)
}
```

The student plans to use the procedure for clubs, tutoring sessions, and dance rehearsals. Which statement best explains why using parameters in the procedure is helpful?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.optionA: It allows the same procedure to be used for different flyers without rewriting the algorithm each time.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.optionB: It guarantees that every flyer will be displayed in the same order on every screen.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.optionC: It automatically stores all flyer information in a list for later use.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.optionD: It removes the need to check whether the title, date, and room values are correct.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.explanation:
The correct answer is A because parameters make the procedure general enough to work with different input values. The procedure can create many different flyers by passing in different titles, dates, and room numbers, which reduces duplicated code and makes the algorithm easier to reuse.

B is incorrect because parameters do not guarantee screen order; they only let the procedure accept different values.

C is incorrect because the procedure displays values, but it does not automatically create a list or store the data for later use.

D is incorrect because parameters do not eliminate the need to verify that the inputs are correct; the procedure still depends on valid values.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.question: A procedure must rotate a list one position to the right, moving the last value to the first position and shifting every other value one position right. The list contains at least two values, uses 1-based indexing, and assignments take effect immediately. Which procedure correctly performs the rotation while preserving every original value?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.optionA:
```text
PROCEDURE rotateRight(items)
  n <- LENGTH(items)
  saved <- items[n]
  i <- n
  REPEAT n - 1 TIMES
    items[i] <- items[i - 1]
    i <- i - 1
  items[1] <- saved
END PROCEDURE
```
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.optionB:
```text
PROCEDURE rotateRight(items)
  n <- LENGTH(items)
  saved <- items[1]
  i <- 1
  REPEAT n - 1 TIMES
    items[i] <- items[i + 1]
    i <- i + 1
  items[n] <- saved
END PROCEDURE
```
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.optionC:
```text
PROCEDURE rotateRight(items)
  n <- LENGTH(items)
  saved <- items[n]
  i <- 2
  REPEAT n - 1 TIMES
    items[i] <- items[i - 1]
    i <- i + 1
  items[1] <- saved
END PROCEDURE
```
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.optionD:
```text
PROCEDURE rotateRight(items)
  n <- LENGTH(items)
  saved <- items[n]
  i <- n - 1
  REPEAT n - 1 TIMES
    items[i] <- items[i + 1]
    i <- i - 1
  items[1] <- saved
END PROCEDURE
```
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.explanation:
Option A is correct. It saves the last value before changing the list, then copies each earlier value one position to the right, starting at the end. Copying backward prevents a value from being overwritten before it is copied. Finally, the saved last value is placed at the first position.

Option B performs a left rotation: it saves the first value, shifts later values left, and places the saved value at the end.

Option C copies values from left to right. Each assignment overwrites a value that the next assignment needs, so the original values are not preserved.

Option D copies values in the wrong direction, from each position to the position before it. This overwrites values and does not shift the original values right as required.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.question: A student team updates a food-ordering app by adding a feature that saves favorite meals. After the update, they rerun tests for placing an order, saving an order, and canceling an order that had already passed before the change. What development practice are they using, and why is it useful?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.optionA: Regression testing, because it helps determine whether new changes broke existing features
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.optionB: Boundary testing, because it checks whether the app works only at its smallest and largest inputs
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.optionC: User-centered testing, because it collects opinions about whether the new feature is appealing
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.optionD: Version tracking, because it automatically restores earlier versions of the app after each update
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-3.explanation:
Regression testing means rerunning previously successful tests after a change to make sure existing functionality still works. In this scenario, the team added a new feature and then retested older features to check for unintended side effects.

A is correct because regression testing helps catch bugs introduced by updates.

B is incorrect because boundary testing focuses on edge values, not on retesting old features after a change.

C is incorrect because user-centered testing is about gathering feedback from users, not verifying that prior functions still work.

D is incorrect because version tracking records changes over time; it does not automatically test or restore the app.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.question: A team is developing a hiking app that shows trail maps and restroom locations. Many users report that cell service is unreliable in the park. Which design choice best helps the app still work when the network connection is lost?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.optionA: Require the app to load every map and location from the server each time the user opens it.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.optionB: Store recently used map and location data on the device so it can be shown without a connection.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.optionC: Use larger icons and brighter colors so the screen is easier to read outdoors.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.optionD: Split the app into more procedures so the program is easier for developers to read.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.explanation:
B is correct because storing recently used data on the device reduces the app’s dependence on an active network connection. That design choice directly addresses the problem of unreliable cell service and improves usability in the park.

A is incorrect because it makes the app depend even more on a stable connection, so it would fail when service is weak or unavailable.

C is incorrect because better colors and icons may improve readability, but they do not help the app function without network access.

D is incorrect because organizing the program into more procedures may help development, but it does not solve the connectivity problem faced by users.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.question: A device sends a 7-bit value followed by one even-parity bit. The sender transmits $10110100$, where the final bit is the parity bit. The receiver gets $10100100$. What can the receiver conclude from checking the parity?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.optionA: The receiver can identify the changed data bit because the parity bit indicates its position.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.optionB: The data is intact because the received parity bit is $0$, the value used by the sender.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.optionC: An odd number of bits changed, but parity alone cannot identify or correct the changed bit.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.optionD: At least one bit changed, because any number of bit changes makes the parity check fail.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.explanation:
The sent bits contain four $1$s, so the sender appends $0$ to make the total number of $1$s even. The received bits contain three $1$s, so the receiver's even-parity check fails. A parity mismatch indicates an odd number of bit changes, but it does not reveal which bit changed or how to correct it.

A: A single parity bit signals a mismatch but does not locate an error.

B: The receiver must check the parity of all received bits; a parity bit of $0$ does not guarantee the data is intact.

D: An even number of bit changes preserves the parity, so a parity check does not detect every possible error.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.question: A sensor logs elapsed seconds during a $24$-minute test. Its software stores the count in a fixed-width unsigned binary field, which must represent every value from $0$ through $1{,}439$, inclusive. What is the minimum number of bits required for the field?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.explanation: An unsigned field with $n$ bits can represent $2^n$ distinct values, from $0$ through $2^n-1$. A $10$-bit field represents only $1{,}024$ values, ending at $1{,}023$, so it is too small. An $11$-bit field represents $2{,}048$ values, ending at $2{,}047$, which includes every required count. A $9$-bit field has an even smaller range, while $12$ bits would work but would not be the minimum.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.question: Two uncompressed, single-channel digital recordings have the same duration. Recording A stores $44{,}100$ samples per second using $8$ bits per sample. Recording B stores $22{,}050$ samples per second using $16$ bits per sample. Which statement correctly compares the recordings?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.optionA: Recording A can represent more amplitude levels per sample, and its binary data is larger.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.optionB: Recording A samples the sound more frequently, Recording B can represent more amplitude levels per sample, and both use the same number of bits for the same duration.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.optionC: Recording B samples the sound more frequently, but both recordings can represent the same number of amplitude levels per sample.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.optionD: Recording B can represent more amplitude levels per sample, so it must use more bits for the same duration.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.explanation:
A higher sample rate means measurements are taken more frequently, while a higher bit depth allows more possible amplitude values for each sample. For the same duration, the number of bits per second is equal: Recording A uses $44{,}100 \times 8 = 352{,}800$ bits per second, and Recording B uses $22{,}050 \times 16 = 352{,}800$ bits per second.
A is incorrect because Recording A has the lower bit depth, so it represents fewer amplitude levels per sample; the recordings also have equal data sizes.
B is correct: A samples more frequently, B represents more amplitude levels per sample, and their equal products give equal data sizes.
C is incorrect because A, not B, has the higher sample rate; B also has the higher bit depth.
D is incorrect because B's higher bit depth is balanced by its lower sample rate, so the total number of bits is not greater.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.question: A student opens a photo-editing application that is stored on a laptop's solid-state drive (SSD). The operating system loads the application’s instructions into random-access memory (RAM), and the processor executes those instructions. Which statement best describes the roles of these components?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.optionA: The application is hardware because it is stored on the SSD, while the processor is software because it follows instructions.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.optionB: The application is software, while the SSD, RAM, and processor are hardware with different roles in storing and processing instructions.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.optionC: The application is software, and the RAM permanently stores its instructions while the SSD temporarily processes them.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.optionD: The application is software, but the processor only stores its instructions; the RAM executes them while the SSD displays the results.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-4.explanation:
The application is software: a set of instructions. The SSD is hardware that stores data persistently, RAM is hardware that holds instructions and data for active use, and the processor is hardware that executes instructions.

A is incorrect because being stored on hardware does not make software itself hardware, and the processor is not software.

B is correct because it identifies the application as software and distinguishes the hardware components’ roles.

C is incorrect because RAM is typically used for temporary active storage, while the SSD stores data persistently; the SSD does not process instructions.

D is incorrect because the processor executes instructions, RAM stores active instructions and data, and the SSD does not display results.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.question: A grocery chain introduces software that sets discounts for food nearing its expiration date. The chain claims the software both reduces food waste and makes groceries more affordable. Its report says unsold produce fell by 25% and app users paid an average of 10% less for discounted items than the previous month. The software uses purchase histories and location data, and its vendor says the algorithm is proprietary. Which response best evaluates the chain’s claims while considering possible societal impacts?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.optionA: Accept the report as sufficient evidence because lower unsold inventory and lower prices for app users demonstrate both claimed benefits for shoppers overall.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.optionB: Treat the waste result as promising, but require the chain to publish the full source code before considering any evidence about affordability or privacy.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.optionC: Treat the report as preliminary; independently compare total waste and actual grocery costs across comparable stores and customer groups, and review data practices under confidentiality.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.optionD: Reject both claims because using purchase histories and location data necessarily violates privacy, and a proprietary algorithm cannot be evaluated ethically.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.explanation:
The report offers some evidence of reduced unsold produce, but it does not establish the overall effect on waste or affordability. App users and discounted items may not represent all shoppers, and a lower price for selected items does not show that shoppers’ total grocery costs fell. Comparing comparable stores and customer groups can reveal whether benefits are distributed equitably. Reviewing what data is collected and how it is protected addresses privacy. An independent reviewer can examine the algorithm and results under confidentiality, so the vendor’s intellectual-property claim need not prevent evaluation.
A. The reported averages do not establish benefits for shoppers overall or show that total grocery costs fell.
B. Publishing source code is not the only way to evaluate a claim; a confidential independent review can protect intellectual property while testing the claims.
D. Collecting location and purchase data raises privacy concerns that should be examined, but does not by itself prove a privacy violation. A proprietary system can still be evaluated.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.question: A student team is creating a mobile app for their school that helps students find available study rooms. They have limited time before the project deadline. Which development choice best follows an effective design and development process?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.optionA: Build decorative animations first so the app looks complete before any testing is done.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.optionB: Create a simple working version with the main room-search feature, test it against the requirements, and then add extra features if time remains.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.optionC: Add as many features as possible at once, even if the team cannot verify whether the app works correctly.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.optionD: Wait until the final day to try the app so that users only see the finished product once.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.explanation:
The best choice is 
B. In an effective design and development cycle, the team should first build a small working prototype that addresses the core problem. Testing the main feature early helps them confirm that the artifact meets the most important requirements before spending time on optional additions.

A is incorrect because visual polish does not verify that the app solves the user’s problem.

C is incorrect because adding many features at once makes it harder to test, debug, and determine whether the artifact actually works.

D is incorrect because waiting until the end prevents early testing and makes it more difficult to fix problems before the deadline.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.question: A student team is planning a computational artifact for the school tutoring center. Before they begin coding, they want to write a success criterion that will help them judge whether the artifact actually solves the problem. Which criterion is the best example of a clear, measurable design goal?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.optionA: The artifact should look modern and use the school colors throughout the interface.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.optionB: The artifact should let a student search by subject and find an available tutor in less than 2 minutes.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.optionC: The artifact should collect a student's interests so it can suggest unrelated clubs and events.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.optionD: The artifact should include every possible tutoring feature before it is shared with users.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.explanation:
The best choice is

B. It is specific and measurable: the team can test whether a student can search by subject and find an available tutor within a time limit. That makes it a useful success criterion during the design process.

A is not as strong because "look modern" is subjective and does not show whether the artifact solves the tutoring problem.

C is unrelated to the stated problem and adds data that is not needed to meet the goal.

D describes adding many features, but that is not a clear success criterion and does not tell the team whether the artifact works well for users.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.question: A company sells a generative image tool to schools and claims that it respects artists’ intellectual property because each image is created in response to a new prompt. Which approach would best evaluate that claim before a school adopts the tool?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.optionA: Review independent evidence about the training images’ sources and permissions, and test whether outputs closely reproduce existing works.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.optionB: Confirm that each student enters a different prompt, since unique prompts ensure that the resulting images are original.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.optionC: Check whether the tool’s website allows anyone to view its outputs, since publicly viewable images cannot violate artists’ rights.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.optionD: Survey students about whether they enjoy the images, since positive reactions show that the tool respects artists’ intellectual property.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.explanation:
A is correct because a new prompt alone does not establish that a system’s training data was used with permission or that its outputs do not closely reproduce existing works. Reviewing data sources and permissions and testing outputs provide relevant evidence for evaluating the company’s claim and the tool’s potential effects on artists.
B is incorrect because different prompts do not guarantee original outputs or establish that training images were used appropriately.
C is incorrect because public access to an output does not demonstrate that the underlying training data or the output respects intellectual property.
D is incorrect because student enjoyment measures user satisfaction, not whether artists’ rights or interests are respected.

ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.question: A student team is building a mobile app for managing club event sign-ups. After adding a new reminder feature, the team notices that the app no longer saves some sign-ups correctly. Which development practice would most directly help the team recover quickly and continue improving the computational artifact?
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.optionA: Keep labeled earlier versions of the app so the team can compare changes and return to a working revision if needed.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.optionB: Wait to test the app until every planned feature has been added to the final product.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.optionC: Rewrite the entire app from scratch so that the earlier mistake cannot appear again.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.optionD: Delete older drafts so the portfolio shows only the final version of the app.
ap-computer-science-principles/unit-5.explanation:
Keeping labeled earlier versions supports iterative development because the team can compare revisions, identify when the problem appeared, and restore a working version if necessary.

A is correct because revision history helps developers manage change and recover from errors without losing all prior work.

B is incorrect because delaying testing makes it harder to find which change caused the problem.

C is incorrect because starting over wastes time and does not help isolate the bug.

D is incorrect because older drafts can be useful for showing development progress and diagnosing problems, even if they are not part of the final product.

ap-english-language/unit-1.question: A regional public library system is publishing a brief webpage after receiving reports that scammers are calling patrons and demanding immediate payment of fake overdue fines by text message or gift cards. The webpage must address a broad audience of adults with different levels of technological confidence. Which opening best fits the rhetorical situation by establishing an effective speaker persona for this purpose and context?
ap-english-language/unit-1.optionA: As your library, we want to make one thing clear: we will never demand payment by text message, gift card, or phone call. If you receive such a request, please contact us directly before taking any action.
ap-english-language/unit-1.optionB: According to municipal collections procedures, all outstanding account balances should be verified through the approved payment portal before remittance is authorized.
ap-english-language/unit-1.optionC: It is frustrating that so many people fall for obvious scams, but the public should have known better than to trust any message about overdue fines.
ap-english-language/unit-1.optionD: We are pleased to announce that our organization remains committed to excellence in information services, community outreach, and the continued growth of our patron experience.
ap-english-language/unit-1.explanation:
A is correct because it matches the rhetorical situation: the exigence is an active scam threat, the audience is broad and varied, and the purpose is to warn clearly and quickly. The speaker persona is calm, trustworthy, and helpful, which is appropriate for a public-facing library message.

B is incorrect because it sounds bureaucratic and technical. That speaker persona fits internal policy writing better than a public warning meant for a general audience.

C is incorrect because it blames the audience and creates an alienating tone. A warning about scams should build trust and reduce confusion, not shame readers.

D is incorrect because it is vague and promotional. It does not address the specific exigence or give the audience the concrete guidance they need.

ap-english-language/unit-1.question: A regional air-quality scientist writes in a monthly bulletin for residents: “This month’s map shows fewer high-pollution readings, but two monitors were offline during the heat wave. The map includes only functioning stations, so it cannot establish that exposure fell in every neighborhood. We are publishing the map now because residents need current information to plan outdoor activities; we will update it when the monitors are repaired.” Which interpretation best explains the scientist’s qualification of the map’s results?
ap-english-language/unit-1.optionA: The scientist balances the need for timely information with gaps in the data, limiting the conclusion to what the evidence supports.
ap-english-language/unit-1.optionB: The scientist shifts responsibility for interpreting the map entirely to residents by avoiding any explanation of its results.
ap-english-language/unit-1.optionC: The scientist implies that the monitor failures make all current air-quality readings unreliable and therefore useless.
ap-english-language/unit-1.optionD: The scientist aims to persuade officials that the monitor failures do not matter because the map is still being published.
ap-english-language/unit-1.explanation:
A is correct. The scientist’s context—a heat wave, offline monitors, and residents’ immediate need for information—creates a tension between publishing promptly and making a fully supported claim. By stating what the map cannot establish, the scientist adopts a cautious stance that supports credibility while still serving the bulletin’s practical purpose.

B is incorrect because the scientist explains how the missing data limit the conclusion rather than leaving residents to interpret the limitation alone.

C is incorrect because the scientist does not dismiss all readings; the map still reports data from functioning stations.

D is incorrect because the scientist acknowledges that monitor failures matter and promises an update after repairs, rather than arguing that the failures are inconsequential.

ap-english-language/unit-1.question:
A state-park naturalist posts the following notice before an annual meteor-viewing event:

“Since the observatory opened, visitors have asked why the ridge trail closes at dusk during the August meteor watch. I understand the frustration: a dark trail seems like the best place to see meteors. Yet volunteer observers record the faintest streaks from the ridge, and even a brief phone screen can interfere with their night vision. The closure applies only on those two nights; the lower meadow remains open, and staff will lead short viewing walks there. You need not take our word for it: try leaving your phone in your pocket for ten minutes at the meadow and notice what becomes visible. Then tell us whether the signs made the reason for the closure clear.”

Which interpretation best explains how the naturalist’s rhetorical choices respond to the audience and context?
ap-english-language/unit-1.optionA: The naturalist mainly aims to establish that visitors lack the expertise to question park rules, using professional authority to discourage further discussion.
ap-english-language/unit-1.optionB: The naturalist seeks visitors’ cooperation with a temporary closure by recognizing their frustration, explaining the reason, and offering an alternative that supports the policy’s credibility.
ap-english-language/unit-1.optionC: The naturalist primarily informs visitors about the observatory’s research methods, avoiding persuasion so that readers can decide whether the closure is necessary.
ap-english-language/unit-1.optionD: The naturalist tries to persuade visitors that phone use is harmful in all outdoor settings, using the event to advocate a broad restriction on devices.
ap-english-language/unit-1.explanation:
B is correct. The notice responds to visitors who see the ridge as an appealing viewing spot by acknowledging their frustration, limiting the closure to two nights, and describing an alternative. The invitation to test the effect of phone light also makes the explanation feel open to visitors’ experience rather than relying only on authority.

A is incorrect because the naturalist does not dismiss questions or claim that visitors lack expertise; the notice invites feedback. C is incorrect because the explanation of observation practices supports a clear persuasive aim: gaining cooperation with the closure. D is incorrect because the naturalist addresses phone screens in the specific context of night-sky viewing, not as a reason for a general device ban.

ap-english-language/unit-1.question: Ahead of a local election, voters have questioned a county election office’s redesigned ballot-return envelope. The office’s communications director writes: “Our office chose to place the signature panel on the back of the envelope after testing several layouts. State law requires a voter’s signature, but it does not dictate where the panel must appear. We placed it on the back to keep the address and barcode unobstructed. The new layout cannot prevent every error, so we will also post an annotated example and provide staff to answer questions.” Which explanation best describes how the director’s account of the situation shapes the passage’s persuasive stance?
ap-english-language/unit-1.optionA: By distinguishing the office’s design choices from legal requirements and acknowledging a limit of the redesign, the director addresses voter concerns without overstating what the office can guarantee.
ap-english-language/unit-1.optionB: By emphasizing that state law requires a signature, the director assigns the design decision to lawmakers and avoids taking responsibility for the envelope’s layout.
ap-english-language/unit-1.optionC: By citing tests of several layouts, the director claims the new envelope will prevent errors and implies that voters no longer need additional guidance.
ap-english-language/unit-1.optionD: By withholding the reasons for the design and referring voters to later instructions, the director avoids engaging with public criticism of the office’s decision.
ap-english-language/unit-1.explanation:
A is correct. The director clarifies which part of the process is legally required and which part the office chose, then acknowledges that the redesign cannot eliminate every error. In the context of voter questions, this candor supports credibility while helping the office explain its decision and offer practical guidance.

B is incorrect because the director explicitly says the law does not dictate the panel’s location and identifies the office as responsible for choosing it.

C is incorrect because the director does not present testing as proof that errors will be prevented; the stated limitation and added guidance make the opposite clear.

D is incorrect because the director directly answers why the panel is placed on the back rather than avoiding the criticism.

ap-english-language/unit-1.question:
A university admissions director publishes the following statement for applicants placed on the wait list:

“Each spring, our office receives requests for a wait-list number. We do not assign a single ranked position. A place may open in one program but not another, and the size and mix of the incoming class are not settled until admitted students respond. For that reason, we cannot calculate a reliable personal probability from an applicant’s file, and we will not imply that a particular update can move someone forward. Applicants who want to remain on the list should use the form by May 1; beyond that, please make plans with another institution. We know this is an unsatisfying answer when you are deciding where to live and study. But a precise-sounding number would suggest certainty our process does not have. We will send an update as soon as decisions are final.”

Which best explains how the director’s refusal to provide individual probability estimates serves the statement’s purpose?
ap-english-language/unit-1.optionA: It recognizes applicants’ desire for certainty while avoiding a claim the admissions process cannot support, which helps preserve the office’s credibility.
ap-english-language/unit-1.optionB: It shifts responsibility for the wait-list outcome to applicants, encouraging them to accept the university’s decisions without asking further questions.
ap-english-language/unit-1.optionC: It suggests that applicants can improve their chances by submitting additional updates, even though the office does not explicitly request them.
ap-english-language/unit-1.optionD: It reassures applicants that the office has already determined the final class, presenting the wait list as a formality rather than an active process.
ap-english-language/unit-1.explanation:
The director addresses an audience making consequential plans and likely seeking a clear ranking or estimate. By explaining why the office cannot offer a reliable probability, the director acknowledges that audience concern while avoiding false precision; this supports the informative purpose and the office’s credibility.

B is incorrect because the statement does not ask applicants to accept a decision without question; it explains a limit in what the office can know.

C is incorrect because the director specifically says an update will not imply that an applicant can move forward and gives no request to submit additional materials.

D is incorrect because the statement says the class is not settled until admitted students respond and promises a later update, indicating that the process is still active.

ap-english-language/unit-2.question:
A student is drafting a letter to the school board advocating for the installation of water-bottle refill stations in the cafeteria. The student wants the argument to appeal to a skeptical audience by using Ethos and Logos while maintaining a calm, persuasive Tone. Which revision of the underlined sentence would best strengthen the argument?

"Installing refill stations would be a smart choice for our school."
ap-english-language/unit-2.optionA: "According to the district’s facilities report, each station would cost about $2,000 and could reduce thousands of plastic bottles each year, making the investment practical as well as responsible."
ap-english-language/unit-2.optionB: "Anyone who cares about the future should be outraged that our cafeteria still wastes bottle after bottle; if the board refuses, it will be choosing waste over wisdom."
ap-english-language/unit-2.optionC: "As a student and member of the Environmental Club, I can say this idea matters to me, and many students would probably appreciate it if the board approved it."
ap-english-language/unit-2.optionD: "Installing refill stations would be a modern improvement because it is helpful, positive, and exactly the kind of change a school should make."
ap-english-language/unit-2.explanation:
A is correct because it combines Logos with Ethos in a measured Tone. The reference to the district’s facilities report makes the claim credible, and the cost and waste data provide concrete logical support.

B is incorrect because it relies mainly on Pathos and confrontational diction like "outraged" and "waste over wisdom," which may alienate a skeptical audience.

C is incorrect because it uses Ethos through the writer’s role, but the personal testimony is too limited and tentative; "probably" weakens the Logos and makes the argument less convincing.

D is incorrect because it uses vague positive diction rather than specific evidence. Its Tone is upbeat, but it lacks the factual support needed to persuade a skeptical school board.

ap-english-language/unit-2.question: A student compares two texts addressing factory safety inspections. A 1910 newspaper editorial states, “I have seen the mill floors at dawn, and I know that a watchful inspector can prevent needless suffering.” A present-day city health department FAQ states, “Our estimate is based on 18 months of inspection logs. It excludes injuries that were not reported; the dataset and calculation method are available for public review.” Which analysis best explains how the FAQ establishes credibility differently from the editorial?
ap-english-language/unit-2.optionA: The editorial relies on logos because it refers to an inspector, while the FAQ relies on pathos because it mentions injuries.
ap-english-language/unit-2.optionB: The editorial builds ethos through firsthand experience, while the FAQ builds ethos through transparent sourcing and acknowledgment of limits.
ap-english-language/unit-2.optionC: The editorial builds pathos through its reference to suffering, while the FAQ avoids appeals by presenting neutral information.
ap-english-language/unit-2.optionD: The editorial and FAQ use the same ethical appeal because both discuss inspections, though the FAQ has a more formal tone.
ap-english-language/unit-2.explanation:
The editorial asks readers to trust the writer’s personal observation, an ethical appeal based on firsthand experience. The FAQ establishes credibility differently by identifying its evidence, explaining a limitation, and making its method available for scrutiny.
A is incorrect because merely mentioning an inspector does not make the editorial’s appeal primarily logical, and the FAQ’s reference to injuries describes a data limitation rather than an attempt to evoke emotion.
C is incorrect because the editorial’s reference to suffering may have emotional force, but the question asks how the FAQ builds credibility; presenting information does not mean it avoids rhetorical appeals.
D is incorrect because the texts do not rely on the same basis for credibility: one invokes personal witness, while the other emphasizes transparent evidence and method.

ap-english-language/unit-2.question:
A student compares two short appeals for language study.

**A. Municipal evening-school pamphlet, 1913:** “A clerk who can read a supplier’s instructions without waiting for an interpreter can prevent a costly delay. Language study, then, is not ornament but equipment for work.”

**B. Language-learning app welcome screen, 2024:** “Think of learning a language as tuning an instrument: a brief practice today makes tomorrow’s phrase easier to hear and shape. Begin with one conversation, not a promise of instant fluency.”

Which analysis best evaluates the appeals and reasoning in the two excerpts?
ap-english-language/unit-2.optionA: Excerpt A relies chiefly on ethos because it assumes the authority of municipal educators, while excerpt B relies on pathos by using an artistic comparison.
ap-english-language/unit-2.optionB: Both excerpts rely chiefly on logos: A moves from a practical cause-and-effect example to a conclusion, while B uses an analogy to explain gradual progress; neither example proves that language study always produces the promised result.
ap-english-language/unit-2.optionC: Excerpt A relies chiefly on pathos because it warns of delay, while excerpt B uses logos to prove that brief practice will reliably lead to fluency.
ap-english-language/unit-2.optionD: Both excerpts rely chiefly on logos, and their reasoning is equally conclusive because each presents a concrete example of how language study improves communication.
ap-english-language/unit-2.explanation:
B is the best analysis. Excerpt A uses a practical cause-and-effect scenario—a clerk’s ability to read instructions may prevent delay—to support the claim that language study is useful for work. Its movement from example to conclusion gives the pamphlet a formal, utilitarian tone. Excerpt B uses the analogy of tuning an instrument to make gradual practice understandable, then shifts to a conversational invitation. These are both logical appeals, but the example and analogy illustrate the claims rather than prove that the benefits will occur in every case.

A is incorrect because neither excerpt chiefly establishes the speaker’s credibility; the musical analogy in B does not by itself make the appeal emotional. 

C is incorrect because the possible delay in A serves as part of a practical causal argument, and B explicitly avoids promising that practice will reliably produce fluency. 

D is incorrect because the excerpts offer illustrative reasoning, not conclusive evidence; the scenarios do not establish how often the claimed benefits occur.

ap-english-language/unit-2.question: A nonprofit director is revising a grant application to a county foundation for funding a free adult-literacy program at the public library. The paragraph now claims only that the program "has already shown promise" and that "more support would let it reach more adults." Which revision would most effectively strengthen the argument's Ethos and Logos while maintaining an appropriate Tone?
ap-english-language/unit-2.optionA: "Our program can change lives, and anyone who cares about literacy should feel moved to help before another neighbor is left behind."
ap-english-language/unit-2.optionB: "In the pilot session, 42 adults enrolled, 31 completed the course, and 18 have since asked for tutoring, evidence that the program is already meeting a documented need."
ap-english-language/unit-2.optionC: "Unlike less serious initiatives, our staff obviously knows how to fix the city's literacy crisis, so the foundation ought to trust our judgment."
ap-english-language/unit-2.optionD: "If the foundation declines this request, it will be choosing to ignore the shameful reality that struggling readers in our city are being abandoned."
ap-english-language/unit-2.explanation:
Option B is the strongest revision because it uses Logos by providing specific, concrete evidence from the pilot session and also builds Ethos by showing the program has real results. Its Diction is precise and its Tone is professional, which is appropriate for a grant application to a skeptical audience.

A is weaker because it relies mostly on Pathos; it asks readers to feel sympathy but offers no evidence.

C is ineffective because its Diction is arrogant and dismissive, which harms Ethos and creates an off-putting Tone.

D is also too dependent on Pathos. The accusatory, shame-based Tone may alienate the foundation instead of persuading it with clear reasoning.

ap-english-language/unit-2.question:
Read the two fictional excerpts.

**Excerpt 1: From an 1896 weather bureau circular**
“For twelve years, the Bureau has compared winter observations from counties across the region. A single report may describe one valley; a record kept by many observers can reveal a regional pattern. Keep a daily note of the first snowfall and send your register to the Bureau each spring.”

**Excerpt 2: From a contemporary weather app notification**
“Your morning should belong to you, not to a surprise downpour. Join 800,000 commuters who check Stormline before leaving. Set a location alert in seconds.”

Which analysis best evaluates how the excerpts use appeals and arrangement to persuade their audiences?
ap-english-language/unit-2.optionA: The circular establishes institutional credibility and explains the value of combined observations before making its request; the notification foregrounds convenience and urgency, while its user count suggests popularity rather than forecast accuracy.
ap-english-language/unit-2.optionB: Both excerpts rely primarily on logical proof: the circular’s years of records and the notification’s user count provide equally direct evidence that each service makes accurate predictions.
ap-english-language/unit-2.optionC: The circular chiefly uses emotional appeal through its reference to a valley, while the notification chiefly uses ethical appeal because commuters are presented as trustworthy authorities.
ap-english-language/unit-2.optionD: The notification makes the stronger logical case because it offers a quick action, while the circular weakens its credibility by asking ordinary observers to contribute information.
ap-english-language/unit-2.explanation:
The circular first invokes the Bureau’s twelve-year record, then explains why observations gathered across counties can reveal patterns, and only afterward asks readers to contribute. This sequence supports institutional ethos and a logos-based explanation. The notification opens with the emotionally appealing promise of avoiding a disruption and emphasizes ease and popularity; the figure of 800,000 users indicates adoption, not that the forecasts are accurate.

B is incorrect because a large user count does not directly prove forecast accuracy, so the two excerpts do not offer equivalent logical evidence.

C is incorrect because the reference to a valley illustrates the limits of one observation rather than primarily appealing to emotion, and commuters are not presented as authorities on the app’s reliability.

D is incorrect because a quick action is a convenience, not evidence that a forecast is accurate. Asking observers to contribute does not by itself undermine the Bureau’s credibility; the circular explains how their reports contribute to a broader record.

ap-english-language/unit-3.question: A local historical society is debating whether to digitize its collection of six hundred nineteenth-century maps. In an editorial supporting the project, a writer claims that digitization will broaden public access and preserve the originals. The writer cites the society’s inquiry log, which records that eighteen of the twenty-five map requests received last year came from people outside the county. The writer also cites interviews with three archivists at regional institutions who say that high-resolution scans allow researchers to examine maps remotely. In an email poll sent by the society, five of eight responding teachers said they would use digital maps in class. A board member argues that the project’s cost could divert money from humidity controls, and that scanning requires staff to handle the originals. Which evaluation of the writer’s evidence and reasoning is most defensible?
ap-english-language/unit-3.optionA: The records and interviews prove that digitization will substantially increase public use and protect the originals, while the small teacher poll confirms broad classroom demand.
ap-english-language/unit-3.optionB: The inquiry log and archivists’ accounts support a limited claim about remote research access, but the small poll does not establish broad classroom demand, and the preservation claim needs evidence about handling effects and competing conservation costs.
ap-english-language/unit-3.optionC: Because the inquiry log and interviews were collected by interested institutions, they are not credible evidence; the board member’s cost objection is therefore the only reliable basis for a decision.
ap-english-language/unit-3.optionD: The teacher poll is the strongest evidence because it reports intended future use, so the writer can claim that digitization will expand access; the board member’s objection is unrelated to that claim.
ap-english-language/unit-3.explanation:
The inquiry log provides relevant evidence that many recorded requesters were outside the county, and the archivists’ experience offers support for the possibility of remote consultation. Together, they justify a cautious claim about access, but not a prediction of a substantial increase in use. The teacher poll has only eight respondents, so it cannot establish broad classroom demand. The evidence also does not show that digitization preserves originals: the writer would need information about whether scanning reduces later handling, while the board member raises a relevant competing cost involving humidity controls.

A overstates what a limited request log, three interviews, and a small poll establish, and it asserts a preservation benefit without evidence.

C dismisses relevant evidence solely because of who collected it and treats the cost objection as conclusive, rather than assessing the evidence’s scope and relevance.

D treats a very small poll of responding teachers as representative and overlooks that the cost objection matters to the separate claim that digitization will preserve the originals.

ap-english-language/unit-3.question:
To support a claim that cities should fund neighborhood tool libraries, a student writes:

"Home repairs often get delayed because people need a drill, ladder, or other specialized equipment only once or twice. A 2024 study by the Northeast Housing Cooperative followed 400 residents in two neighborhoods with tool libraries and found that 64% of borrowers completed minor repairs within a week, compared with 38% of residents in similar neighborhoods without the service."

Which sentence would best follow this evidence to provide effective Commentary and Sourcing while strengthening the line of reasoning?
ap-english-language/unit-3.optionA: This study proves that every resident will repair a home faster whenever a tool library opens nearby.
ap-english-language/unit-3.optionB: Because the cooperative tracked similar neighborhoods over time, its comparison makes the evidence more credible and suggests that borrowing tools can help residents finish small repairs before those problems worsen.
ap-english-language/unit-3.optionC: Some people may still prefer to buy their own tools, so the writer should focus on that objection instead of the study.
ap-english-language/unit-3.optionD: Since 400 residents were included, the results must apply to every city, regardless of local conditions.
ap-english-language/unit-3.explanation:
B is correct because it does two important things: it uses Commentary to explain why the evidence matters, and it uses Sourcing to show why the study is credible. The sentence connects the data to the Claim by showing how access to tools can prevent small repairs from becoming larger problems, which advances the line of reasoning.

A is incorrect because it overgeneralizes the evidence. A comparison in one study does not prove that every resident in every setting will respond the same way.

C is incorrect because it introduces a Counterclaim but does not explain how the evidence still supports the Claim. It shifts away from the line of reasoning instead of strengthening it.

D is incorrect because it also overgeneralizes. A sample of 400 residents can be useful evidence, but it does not automatically justify a claim about all cities or all local conditions.

ap-english-language/unit-3.question:
A student is drafting an argument that the city should install shade structures at busy bus stops. The student writes, "Passengers are more likely to wait for buses when the stops offer protection from extreme heat. A six-week pilot in three neighborhoods found that complaints about heat decreased after temporary awnings were installed."

Which sentence would best follow the excerpt to strengthen the student’s line of reasoning?
ap-english-language/unit-3.optionA: Because the pilot was reviewed by an independent public-health researcher, the evidence is credible enough to support the claim, even though some critics argue that shade structures could make curbside sightlines less open.
ap-english-language/unit-3.optionB: Many riders probably appreciate having a cooler place to stand, and the city should do whatever helps them most.
ap-english-language/unit-3.optionC: The pilot proves that every bus stop in the city needs the same awnings immediately.
ap-english-language/unit-3.optionD: The report is interesting, and the city should keep looking for ways to help riders in hot weather.
ap-english-language/unit-3.explanation:
A is correct because it uses **sourcing** to show why the pilot study is credible and then adds **commentary** that connects the evidence to the **claim**. It also anticipates a **counterclaim** about sightlines without abandoning the argument’s **line of reasoning**.

B is incorrect because it expresses support, but it does not explain why the evidence matters or how it supports the claim in a logical way.

C is incorrect because it overgeneralizes from a limited pilot study; the evidence does not justify claiming that every bus stop should be changed immediately.

D is incorrect because it is vague and does not clearly connect the evidence to the claim. It also fails to address any counterclaim or develop the line of reasoning.

ap-english-language/unit-3.question: A writer argues that the city should attach a plain-language summary to each zoning decision notice while keeping the full technical notice available. The writer cites a city clerk’s audit of all 48 zoning notices issued last year: 31 stated the decision but did not explain its practical effects. The clerk’s office also logged 17 calls from residents seeking clarification, although the logs do not identify what prompted each call. A developers’ association argues that summaries could leave out important restrictions. Which commentary most defensibly connects the evidence to the writer’s claim while addressing the limits of the evidence and the counterargument?
ap-english-language/unit-3.optionA: Because 31 notices omitted practical effects and residents called for clarification, the evidence proves that the notices caused confusion and that summaries will eliminate it; the developers’ objection need not affect the conclusion.
ap-english-language/unit-3.optionB: The clerk’s records are official, so the 17 calls establish that residents cannot understand zoning decisions; the city should replace technical notices with summaries that omit unnecessary restrictions.
ap-english-language/unit-3.optionC: The audit identifies a recurring gap in notices, and the calls suggest a need for clarification, though they do not show what prompted each call. Summaries alongside full notices could address that gap while preserving restrictions the association considers important.
ap-english-language/unit-3.optionD: Because the call logs do not identify why residents called, neither source supports the proposal; the possibility that summaries omit restrictions is enough to show that the city should reject it.
ap-english-language/unit-3.explanation:
C uses the audit as evidence of a specific, recurring omission and treats the call logs cautiously: they suggest a need for clarification but do not establish that the notices caused the calls. It connects those findings to a limited proposal—adding summaries without replacing full notices—which also addresses the developers’ concern about omitted restrictions.

A overstates what the evidence proves: the records do not establish either the cause of the calls or that summaries would eliminate confusion.

B treats official records as proof of residents’ general inability to understand zoning and proposes removing technical details, neither of which the evidence supports.

D treats a limitation in one source as if it invalidates both sources and assumes the counterargument is conclusive without evidence.

ap-english-language/unit-3.question: A student argues that the county should expand its mobile museum-kit program because the kits have improved historical understanding throughout the county. The museum’s annual report states that 11 classes borrowed kits last year and that 9 of the 10 borrowing teachers who completed a feedback form rated them useful. The report notes that only teachers whose classes borrowed kits were surveyed and that student learning was not assessed. Several rural principals have also said that the distance required to pick up kits makes participation difficult. Which commentary would most effectively connect this evidence to a defensible claim?
ap-english-language/unit-3.optionA: Because nearly every surveyed teacher found the kits useful, the program has improved historical understanding across the county, and expanding it will benefit students in every school.
ap-english-language/unit-3.optionB: The report establishes that some classes borrowed kits and participating teachers generally valued them, but it does not demonstrate student learning gains or represent schools unable to participate; the access concern should qualify any case for expansion.
ap-english-language/unit-3.optionC: Because the museum produced the report and surveyed only participating teachers, its evidence is too biased to support any claim about the program, even the limited claim that teachers found the kits useful.
ap-english-language/unit-3.optionD: The 11 borrowing classes show that the program is effective, while rural principals’ concerns are unrelated to the evidence and therefore need not affect the recommendation to expand it.
ap-english-language/unit-3.explanation:
B distinguishes what the evidence supports from what it does not: the report documents borrowing and positive feedback from participating teachers, but it neither measures student learning nor represents schools facing access barriers. That limitation makes a countywide claim about improved understanding too broad and means the access counterargument should be addressed.

A overstates the evidence: teacher perceptions do not establish student learning gains or represent every school.

C dismisses evidence too completely. The report can support a limited claim about borrowing and participating teachers’ feedback even though it cannot establish broader effects.

D treats borrowing as proof of effectiveness and ignores a relevant limitation: schools that face pickup barriers may be missing from the feedback and participation data.

ap-english-language/unit-4.question: A student argues that the city archive should add a neighborhood index to its online collection. The student notes that 62% of a sample of 500 search queries included a neighborhood name, while the current catalog is organized by acquisition year. Which sentence, placed between this evidence and the recommendation, most effectively supplies the missing warrant and improves the argument’s logical progression?
ap-english-language/unit-4.optionA: When many users search by place, a neighborhood index can help them find related records that are otherwise dispersed across acquisition years.
ap-english-language/unit-4.optionB: The archive receives new records every year, so its acquisition-year catalog reflects the history of the collection’s growth.
ap-english-language/unit-4.optionC: Because the most common searches mention neighborhoods, the archive should place the neighborhood with the most searches at the top of its homepage.
ap-english-language/unit-4.optionD: The survey included 500 queries, which means the results describe every search that archive users will make in the future.
ap-english-language/unit-4.explanation:
A links the evidence about how users search to the proposed organizational change: a place-based index can make records easier to locate even when they are spread across years. This supplies the warrant connecting the survey finding to the recommendation.
B adds background about the existing catalog but does not explain why the query data supports a neighborhood index.
C leaps from a common search pattern to featuring one neighborhood, a different recommendation that the evidence does not justify.
D overstates what a sample can establish and does not connect search behavior to the proposed catalog structure.

ap-english-language/unit-4.question:
A student drafting an editorial about improving city services writes the following paragraph:

"To make the permit process more efficient, the city council should launch a digital permit portal. In neighboring Riverton, the portal reduced average wait times from 14 days to 5 days within six months. The council should adopt the same system this year."

Which revision would best improve the paragraph’s organization and logical progression?
ap-english-language/unit-4.optionA: If applicants can submit forms online instead of waiting in line, staff can process requests more quickly, which makes the Riverton data relevant to the council’s decision.
ap-english-language/unit-4.optionB: Although some residents prefer paper forms, online systems often look more modern and appealing.
